newsitem.title: USA: USDA says 5,427 suspect cattle examined for BSE.
newsitem.headline: USDA says 5,427 suspect cattle examined for BSE.

text.p: Agriculture Department scientists have examined the brains of more than 5,427 cattle from nearly all U.S. states and Puerto Rico and found no sign of mad cow disease, a researcher said Tuesday.
"Our monitoring and surveillance system is one of the most aggressive in the world," said Thomas Gomez, a veterinary epidemiologist with the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.
"If this disease is occurring, it's occurring at such a low level that our surveillance would not detect it," Gomez said in an interview.

The USDA began a program in 1990 to monitor and prevent the outbreak of mad cow disease -- known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy or BSE -- among U.S. herds. Scientists had examined brain samples from 5,427 high-risk cattle in 47 states and Puerto Rico through Feb. 28, Gomez said. None showed any sign of the deadly disease.
The United States slaughters about 33 million cows a year and each animal is checked for a variety of possible diseases before slaughter.

The U.S. government banned cattle imports from Britain in 1989, and two years later extended the ban to several other European countries. The USDA has also banned or restricted imports of animal feed, bull semen and fertilized eggs from cows in countries were BSE is known to exist.
The Food and Drug Administration in January proposed an additional rule that would prohibit U.S. meat processors from recycling cattle remains into feed supplements for cows, sheep and goats.
"That's the second firewall that will be put into place by the FDA feed ban," Gomez said. "This will eliminate any potential amplification of the disease."

But Gomez said a ban on using remains from all mammals in cattle food was unnecessary. The stricter rule is supported by some consumer groups and Richard Rhodes, the author of a controversial new book, "Deadly Feasts."

"It would not be warranted based on the scientific data on hand," Gomez said. "With the system we have in place already, any animal exhibiting central nervous system abnormalities would not be allowed to enter the food chain."

APHIS is also monitoring a group of cattle imported from Britain in the 1980s, prior to the U.S. ban. Of the 469 cattle imported, 34 are still alive in the United States. None have become infected with BSE, he said.
